method: S1 and S2 are open RACGP AJGP articles from September 2020, fetched and checked verbatim (20 claims). A1 is AMH, paraphrased, no passage reproduced and no source_text stored (21 claims, 6 doses). THE SOURCES GIVE DIFFERENT REFERRAL THRESHOLDS FOR A NON-HEALING ORAL ULCER: S1 says 2 weeks or more, A1 says consider neoplasia beyond 3 weeks. Both are stated with attribution and the guideline does not split the difference, because the shorter threshold is the safer one for a cancer referral and saying so is a judgement the reader should make with both numbers in front of them. AMH's artificial saliva product table lists branded products with pH values; NO product row is reproduced, and only the clinically actionable rule -- neutral pH for patients with their own teeth -- is carried.

claims.claim: S1 states that mucosal turnover should occur in under 10 days and therefore any persistent ulcer that has been present for 2 weeks or more should be referred to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or oral medicine specialist for biopsy
claims.source_text: Mucosal turnover should occur in <10 days; 2 therefore, any persistent ulcer that has been present for ≥2 weeks should be referred to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or oral medicine specialist for biopsy.

claims.claim: An ulcerated lesion is most commonly traumatic or immunological in origin, but the most important lesion to exclude is an oral malignancy, and persistence as opposed to episodic recurrence of an ulcer is an important feature
claims.source_text: An ulcerated lesion is most commonly traumatic or immunological (aphthous) in origin; however, the most important lesion to exclude is an oral malignancy. … Persistence, as opposed to episodic recurrence, of an ulcer is an importance feature.

claims.claim: The most common oral ulcer is caused by trauma, most often mechanical such as biting but also thermal, radiation or chemical, and the cause must be addressed with review to ensure mucosal healing within two weeks, referring to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon if it persists beyond that period
claims.source_text: The most common oral ulcer is one caused by trauma. This trauma is most often mechanical (eg biting) but may also be from thermal, radiation or chemical means. … The cause must be addressed if possible, and review to ensure mucosal healing within two weeks is recommended. If the ulcer persists beyond this period, referral to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon should be undertaken.

claims.claim: Recurrent aphthous ulceration affects 20 to 50% of the population and presents as painful recurrent ulcers that almost always affect non-keratinised oral mucosa, with three recognised clinical subtypes: minor which is most common, major and herpetiform
claims.source_text: Recurrent aphthous ulceration (otherwise known as recurrent aphthous stomatitis [RAS]) affects 20-50% of the population 3 and presents as painful, recurrent ulcers that almost always affect non-keratinised oral mucosa (buccal mucosa, floor of mouth, vestibule of the lips, soft palate and tongue). The aetiology of RAS is unknown but is thought most likely to be immunologically mediated. 4 There are three recognised clinical subtypes based on their clinical presentation: minor (most common), major and herpetiform.

claims.claim: Minor aphthous ulcers are oval shaped and under 10 mm, frequently last 5 to 10 days and heal without scarring, while major aphthous ulcers are variably shaped and over 10 mm, can last up to six weeks, can heal with scarring, and can resemble an ulcer of an early malignancy
claims.source_text: Minor aphthous ulcers are oval shaped and <10 mm in size, frequently last 5-10 days and heal without scarring (Figure 2). Major aphthous ulcers are variably shaped and >10 mm in size, can last up to six weeks and can heal with scarring. They can resemble an ulcer of an early malignancy.

claims.claim: Herpetiform aphthous ulcers are numerous 1 to 2 mm diameter ulcerations that may coalesce, are not restricted to non-keratinised oral mucosa, and heal in 1 to 2 weeks
claims.source_text: Herpetiform aphthous ulcers are numerous 1-2 mm diameter ulcerations that may coalesce and are not restricted to non-keratinised oral mucosa. They heal in 1-2 weeks.

claims.claim: Aphthous-like ulceration can be associated with haematinic deficiency or gastrointestinal or rheumatological disease, and vitamin B12, folic acid or iron deficiency can be associated with recurrent aphthous stomatitis in a small proportion of patients, so these nutritional markers should be checked and corrected in this subgroup
claims.source_text: Aphthous-like ulceration can be associated with haematinic deficiency or gastrointestinal or rheumatological disease. Vitamin B12, folic acid or iron deficiency can also be associated with RAS in a small proportion of patients, and these nutritional markers should be checked and corrected in this subgroup.

claims.claim: The major risk factors for oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma are smoking, alcohol consumption of more than 3 standard drinks per day and betel quid consumption
claims.source_text: The major risk factors for oral cavity SCC are smoking, 8 alcohol consumption of >3 standard drinks per day 9 and betel quid (paan) consumption.

claims.claim: Oral squamous cell carcinoma most commonly presents as a non-healing ulcer which can be indurated or firm with irregular margins and raised rolled edges, and as it invades adjacent structures may cause neurosensory change and tooth mobility, with alteration of speech and swallowing in late stages
claims.source_text: Oral SCC most commonly presents as a non-healing ulcer, which can be indurated/firm and have irregular margins and raised, rolled edges (Figures 3-6). As SCC invades adjacent structures in the oral cavity, it may result in neurosensory change (paraesthesia or anaesthesia) and tooth mobility. In late stages, it may cause alteration of speech and swallowing.

claims.claim: S1 states that oral squamous cell carcinoma may not necessarily be painful and pain is not used to differentiate between a potentially malignant or benign cause of an ulcer, that it is found across virtually all age groups, and that up to 10% of squamous cell carcinomas are diagnosed in patients who do not smoke or drink alcohol, so the absence of risk factors does not rule out the possibility of malignancy
claims.source_text: It is important to note that oral SCC may not necessarily be painful, and pain is not used to differentiate between a potentially malignant or benign cause of an ulcer. In addition, oral SCC is found across virtually all age groups (including paediatric, although rarely), and up to 10% of SCCs are diagnosed in patients who do not smoke or drink alcohol. 10 Therefore, the absence of risk factors does not rule out the possibility of malignancy.

claims.claim: If an ulcer is suspected to have any suspicious malignant features then immediate referral to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or specialist unit in a tertiary hospital is indicated
claims.source_text: If an ulcer is suspected to have any suspicious malignant features, then immediate referral to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or specialist unit in a tertiary hospital is indicated.

claims.claim: S1 states the possibility of an oral cavity malignancy should always be considered particularly with a non-healing ulcer, a bleeding lesion or an area of mucosa that persistently appears red or white, that leukoplakia and erythroplakia require mandatory referral for biopsy as a significant proportion will be dysplastic or malignant, and that any tissue excised from the oral cavity should be sent for histopathological examination
claims.source_text: The possibility of an oral cavity malignancy should always be considered, particularly with the presentation of a non-healing ulcer, a bleeding lesion or an area of mucosa that persistently appears red or white. - Any persistent ulcer that has been present for ≥2 weeks should be referred to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or oral medicine specialist for biopsy. - Leukoplakia and erythroplakia are clinical terms used to describe oral white and red patches respectively that cannot be scraped off and cannot be ascribed to any disease or condition. Referral for biopsy is mandatory as a significant proportion of these lesions will be dysplastic or malignant. - Any tissue excised from the oral cavity should be sent for histopathological examination as the clinical appearance alone is insufficient to ensure a correct diagnosis.

claims.claim: Lip cancer typically presents as a non-healing ulcer on the vermillion of the lower lip and its management is primarily surgical excision
claims.source_text: Lip cancer typically presents as a non-healing ulcer on the vermillion of the lower lip (Figure 7). The management of lip cancer is primarily surgical excision.

claims.claim: S2 states that once dental infection has spread beyond the confines of the jaws there is an increasing risk of airway obstruction and septicaemia, and that if treated with antibiotics alone the infection will not resolve and will become progressively worse
claims.source_text: Once the infection has spread beyond the confines of the jaws, there is an increasing risk of airway obstruction and septicaemia. If treated with antibiotics alone, the infection will not resolve and will become progressively worse.

claims.claim: S2 states that prompt assessment and referral to a tertiary hospital is required for cases at risk of airway compromise
claims.source_text: Prompt assessment and referral to a tertiary hospital is required for cases at risk of airway compromise.

claims.claim: Patients with dental abscesses commonly initially present to their primary health providers, particularly if they have dental phobia or are financially constrained, and it is easy to underestimate their condition particularly if the infection has spread beyond the confines of the jaws
claims.source_text: Patients with dental abscesses commonly initially present to their primary health providers, particularly if they have dental phobia or are financially constrained. It is easy to underestimate their condition, particularly if the infection has spread beyond the confines of the jaws.

claims.claim: S2 states that in the pre-antibiotic era dental infection was a common cause of death with fatality rates of 10 to 40%, that with antibiotics odontogenic infections responded well to penicillin, and that this may have created a false sense of security while antibiotic-resistant bacteria were generally on the increase
claims.source_text: In the pre-antibiotic era, dental infection was a common cause of death, with fatality rates of 10-40%. 1 With the advent of antibiotics, odontogenic infections responded well to penicillin. This may have created a false sense of security, and such cases were usually treated by junior hospital staff operating out of hours. It may not have been noticed that antibiotic-resistant bacteria were generally on the increase.

claims.claim: S2 reports that a patient with a spreading odontogenic infection died of airway obstruction a few hours after operation at the Royal Adelaide Hospital in 2002, prompting an immediate review and an audit, and that more than 1000 cases of severe odontogenic infection were managed there between 2002 and 2019
claims.source_text: This was the situation at the Royal Adelaide Hospital in 2002 when a patient with a spreading odontogenic infection died of airway obstruction a few hours after operation (Case 1). … Altogether, more than 1000 cases of severe odontogenic infection have been managed at the Royal Adelaide Hospital in the period 2002-19.

claims.claim: S2 states the most dangerous anatomical space is the submandibular space, that when the masseter muscle is irritated by inflammation trismus or difficulty in jaw opening ensues, and that the submandibular space is in direct contact with the pharyngeal spaces and down through the neck to the mediastinum and also connects to the contralateral side
claims.source_text: The most dangerous space is the submandibular space, which is bounded by the mandible laterally, the mylohyoid muscle above and the subcutaneous tissue and skin below. It contains the submandibular gland, lymph nodes and the masseter muscle. When this muscle is irritated by the inflammation, trismus or difficulty in jaw opening ensues. The submandibular space is in direct contact with the pharyngeal spaces and down through the neck to the mediastinum. It also connects to the contralateral side.

claims.claim: S2 states that swelling from the submandibular spaces can extend over a wide area of the airway in both length and breadth, and that Ludwig's angina strictly refers only to cases in which the whole neck bilaterally from the mandible to the clavicle is involved, such cases having a poor prognosis, although the term is commonly misinterpreted to apply to any localised neck infection
claims.source_text: It is essential to understand that swelling from the submandibular spaces can extend over a wide area of the airway in both length and breadth (Figure 1). … Strictly, Ludwig's angina only refers to cases in which the whole neck bilaterally from the mandible to the clavicle is involved in infection. Such cases have a poor prognosis. 6,7 However, the term 'Ludwig's angina' is commonly misinterpreted to apply to any localised neck infection.
